content: The effectiveness of Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) compared to conventional newborn care was evaluated through a systematic review of 27 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) conducted between 1994 and 2021, involving a total of 11,956 infants. Six of these studies were conducted in high-income countries (Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States), four in upper-middle-income countries (China, Colombia, Ecuador, and Malaysia), 15 in lower-middle-income countries (Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, Kenya, and Nepal), and two in a low-income country (Ethiopia). Most studies (25) were conducted in healthcare facilities, while two were community-based. In all but one study, infants were stabilized before enrollment. The initiation of KMC varied: in two studies, it began within 24 hours of birth; in 10 studies, it started between 1 and 7 days after birth; and in 12 studies, it began more than 7 days after birth. Three studies did not report the timing of KMC initiation. The duration of KMC also varied: nine studies reported less than 8 hours per day, nine reported 8–16 hours per day, and four reported more than 16 hours per day. Five studies did not report the duration of KMC. Critical outcomes included all-cause mortality (reported in 16 trials), severe morbidity (reported in 11 trials, including severe infection in 9 trials and hypothermia in 11 trials), growth outcomes such as weight gain (reported in 11 trials), and neurodevelopmental outcomes (reported in 1 trial using Griffith quotients and Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, third edition). No serious adverse events were reported. Subgroup analyses for morbidity, growth, and neurodevelopmental outcomes could not be assessed due to insufficient studies. The analysis of daily KMC duration (<8 hours/day, 8–16 hours/day, and >16 hours/day) was limited by small sample sizes and imprecision. For the comparison of early (<24 hours after birth) versus later (≥24 hours after birth) initiation of KMC, evidence was derived from four RCTs involving 3,603 infants. One study was conducted in a high-income country (Sweden), two in low-income countries (Gambia and Madagascar), and one was a multicountry study conducted in Ghana, India, Malawi, Nigeria, and Tanzania. All studies were conducted in healthcare facilities. Two studies enrolled infants regardless of clinical stability, one enrolled only stable infants, and one enrolled only unstable infants. KMC was initiated as soon as possible after birth in all studies, with initiation occurring between 6 and 19 hours after birth in three studies. One study did not report the timing of KMC initiation. The duration of KMC was less than 8 hours in one study, more than 16 hours in two studies, and not reported in one study. Critical outcomes for early versus later KMC initiation included all-cause mortality (reported in three trials), morbidity (reported in three trials, including severe infection in two trials and hypothermia in three trials), and growth outcomes such as weight gain (reported in one trial). No neurodevelopmental outcomes were reported. Subgroup analyses for morbidity, growth, and neurodevelopmental outcomes could not be assessed due to insufficient studies. Families of preterm or low-birth-weight (LBW) infants expressed a desire to be actively involved in their infants' care, including skin-to-skin contact and feeding. Caregivers' perspectives on KMC highlighted the importance of social support, access to care, and cultural norms in shaping family perceptions, practices, and attitudes toward KMC. Key elements included free services, support from healthcare workers, unrestricted visiting hours, private and quiet spaces for KMC, and the involvement of fathers and partners. Providing KMC was described as both restorative and energy-draining for mothers, fathers, and partners. KMC can be implemented at home and at all levels of newborn care (primary, secondary, and tertiary). Healthcare services should ensure family involvement in the care of preterm or LBW infants, regardless of the infant's clinical condition. Policies should promote zero separation between families and their infants, requiring close collaboration between families and healthcare providers. Healthcare facilities should provide families with access to beds, food, bathing, and toilet facilities during the infant's hospital stay. KMC should ideally be initiated immediately after birth or after initial resuscitation if needed. If the mother is unable to provide KMC, other family members should be prepared to do so. Family members should be identified before delivery, counseled, and allowed access to maternity and newborn care areas. Infants requiring transfer to special or intensive care units should be transported safely in KMC with the mother or another family member. The choice of care location should be guided by the infant's clinical condition, and KMC should be provided even in intensive care units when necessary. Healthcare facilities should support mothers and families to continue KMC at home after discharge. All preterm and LBW infants should be followed up after discharge, ideally through home visits. Infants born at home should receive immediate KMC if they show no danger signs and should be transferred to a healthcare facility if needed. Infrastructure and equipment for KMC include binders to maintain skin-to-skin contact, warm hats, socks, and diapers for infants, and comfortable clothing for caregivers. Reclining beds and chairs may also be helpful. Additional equipment, such as thermometers capable of measuring body temperatures as low as 35°C, is required. If maternal-neonatal intensive care units (M-NICUs) or couplet care units are used, they should have the same infrastructure, equipment, and supplies as NICUs for small or sick infants and maternity wards for mothers. This includes CPAP machines, pulse oximeters, radiant warmers or incubators (if the infant is not in KMC), adult beds, and examination areas for mothers. Healthcare workers at all levels should be trained to support KMC, including helping mothers maintain skin-to-skin contact, assisting with breastfeeding, and providing other neonatal care. They should record the duration of KMC provided per day in clinical registers or home-based records and monitor this regularly. Scaling up KMC should be integrated into national and subnational programs rather than implemented as a standalone intervention. This requires leadership, governance, financing, and health information systems. Leadership should involve high-level policymakers, program managers, and facility directors. Policies should enable zero separation, and pre-service education for healthcare workers should include KMC. Health financing should include dedicated budget lines for KMC and expanded health insurance coverage. Health information systems should monitor KMC coverage and quality at facility, district, and national levels. Facility-based studies have demonstrated the feasibility of providing KMC to small infants for more than 8 hours per day, even immediately after birth, regardless of clinical stability. These studies were conducted in diverse settings, including poor, remote, and urban communities. However, community-initiated KMC and KMC for unstable infants have not been widely implemented outside research settings, and global coverage remains low. The benefits of KMC include reduced mortality (high-certainty evidence), decreased infection and hypothermia (moderate-certainty evidence), increased weight gain (low-certainty evidence), and increased breastfeeding (very-low-certainty evidence). No evidence of harm has been reported.
